The investment rose in its own currency: why your CAD return can still fall

Use four graphics to translate a foreign-currency asset return into CAD, reconcile the interaction term and compare matched currency scenarios.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore a hypothetical unhedged foreign-currency investment

CAD investment value after the selected repeated years$9,509.9

Original hypothetical comparison in nominal CAD. One unhedged foreign-currency asset exposure is purchased at the start, with no additional deposits or withdrawals. The local-currency asset return is a total-return assumption with any distributions reinvested locally. Currency change always means the percentage change in CAD per one foreign currency unit: a positive value raises each foreign unit’s CAD value; a negative value reduces it. The same two annual factors repeat for the selected years, with no probabilities or forecast claim. The unchanged-currency comparator holds the currency quote constant and is not the result of a modeled hedge. No trading or conversion charges, taxes, inflation, borrowing, currency controls or fund-specific exposures are calculated. All values are scenario assumptions, not historical performance or current exchange-rate quotes.

The central idea

The CAD growth factor combines the asset’s local growth factor with the change in CAD per foreign unit. Adding the two percentage changes omits their interaction.

01

State the currency in which you measure the result

An investment can rise in its own currency while declining in the currency used for the household budget. Its local value and the amount of CAD represented by each foreign unit are separate factors. Both affect the CAD value of an unhedged position.

The SEC’s international-investing bulletin explains this general currency risk using a U.S.-dollar perspective. This article applies the same translation principle to original hypothetical CAD examples. It does not reproduce a market return series or assess a particular investment.

The model holds one foreign-currency exposure without additions or withdrawals. Its asset-return assumption includes any distributions reinvested in the foreign currency. It assumes that the exposure is unhedged and excludes taxes, trading charges and conversion fees.

02

Read the exchange-rate quote in the stated direction

The currency control always means the percentage change in CAD per one foreign currency unit. If it is positive, each foreign unit translates into more CAD. If it is negative, each foreign unit translates into fewer CAD.

The Bank of Canada’s daily exchange-rate page expresses one foreign unit converted into CAD and identifies its published rates as indicative. No rate from that page is used in this tool. The controls and examples are independent assumptions, not executable conversion quotes.

For a fictional quote moving from 1.35 CAD per foreign unit to 1.215, the CAD value of each foreign unit falls by 10%. The reciprocal quote rises by about 11.11%, rather than exactly 10%. Reversing the quote changes the denominator as well as the direction, so simply reversing a percentage sign can give the wrong input.

03

Multiply the two growth factors

The one-year CAD return is (1 + local asset return) × (1 + currency change) − 1. In the default case, the asset gains 10% in its foreign currency while CAD per foreign unit falls 10%. The CAD factor is 1.10 × 0.90 = 0.99, producing a 1% decline.

A CAD 10,000 opening position therefore becomes CAD 9,900 after one year, before the excluded costs and taxes. The two percentages do not cancel because the currency translation applies to the ending foreign-currency value, which already includes the asset’s gain.

The one-year waterfall expands the calculation into the opening CAD 10,000, a CAD 1,000 asset effect, a negative CAD 1,000 currency effect on the opening amount and a negative CAD 100 interaction. These four entries reconcile CAD 9,900 without mixing units.

04

Distinguish an unchanged result from opposite percentage signs

For a 10% local asset gain to translate into exactly zero CAD return, the currency factor would need to be 1 ÷ 1.10. That is a decline in CAD per foreign unit of about 9.09%. A 10% decline is slightly larger and produces the default loss.

The fixed matrix shows other one-year combinations. A negative asset return and a positive currency change can partly offset each other, while a negative currency change can deepen an asset loss. The result depends on the pair of factors, not on the asset direction alone.

The matrix assigns no probability to its scenarios. It also does not say that asset and currency returns are independent in observed markets. It isolates the translation arithmetic without estimating their joint behaviour.

05

Use a repeated scenario without mistaking it for an observed path

The default path repeats the same two annual assumptions for five years. The combined CAD factor of 0.99 repeats five times, so CAD 10,000 becomes about CAD 9,509.90. If the currency quote instead remained unchanged, the same hypothetical local asset return would produce about CAD 16,105.10.

The grouped bars keep the entered asset return and starting amount fixed while replacing only the annual currency assumption. Each row has its own stated horizon. This makes the currency sensitivity visible without crediting one scenario with extra deposits or a different local asset performance.

Real annual returns and exchange rates do not need to repeat. These lines connect modeled annual endpoints and contain no historical observations. The unchanged-quote comparison is a counterfactual with a constant exchange rate, not a simulated currency hedge with its own costs and mechanics.

06

Connect the measurement currency to the household goal

A household that will spend CAD needs to understand the position’s CAD value. A household with a future bill in the same foreign currency has a different currency-matching question. The foreign-goal guide separates the bill’s own price from the CAD amount required to fund it.

For an actual account, identify the relevant exposure and the currency in which performance is reported before using a return number in a plan. This tool does not infer the underlying exposures of a fund, measure a company’s operating currencies or choose a hedge.

Finally, allow for the costs and dates of making funds spendable. The illustrated investment values are translated reference amounts. Actual sale proceeds and conversion cash require the applicable prices, charges, taxes and settlement arrangements.

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Charts labelled “Official statistics” or “Derived from official statistics” identify their source periods. Other charts are hypothetical scenarios.
